transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Anand (CTO - Lakeshore), Marcus Lee (SRE), Dana Kim (Product), Tom Reyes (Legal)

Summary: Quick product walkthrough focused on rate limiting, quotas, and org/project key model for multi-tenant controls. Customer concerned about tenant isolation, burst handling, and how to map their internal teams to project keys. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs and security artifacts. Agreed next steps to share pricing, security docs, and run a short pilot with benchmarks.

Topics: rate limits, org/project keys, per-project quotas, billing attribution, SAML/SSO, KMS, SOC2, pilot benchmark plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jenna (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 45 minutes, I'll hand it over to Marco for the console walkthrough in a sec. Priya, you said you wanted to focus on rate limits and how we separate tenants?
[00:18] Priya (Lakeshore): Yeah thanks, mainly around multi-tenant controls. We have a multi-tenant API for clinics and internal teams, we need per-client quotas, ability to throttle bursts, and clear billing attribution. Also need to know how keys map to projects and orgs.
[00:34] Marco (Redwood SE): Totally. We'll demo org vs project keys, show per-key quotas and some of the autoscaling/burst options. Quick note, I'll show the console and then the API examples; there might be a little lag on my screen share so bear with me.
[00:48] Marcus (Lakeshore): Also, on security — KMS integration and audit logs, and whether logs include prompt text or just metadata, that's a big one for us.
[00:57] Jenna: Yep we'll cover that and Marco will point to the security pack we'll send.
[01:10] Marco: Ok sharing screen... (background typing/pauses) Alright, here is the Redwood Console. Top left you can see the org selector, Lakeshore Health would be the org, then you create projects under it for e.g. Clinic-Portal, Billing, Analytics.
[01:30] Marco: Each project gets project keys, these are what you distribute to services. Keys are scoped, so you can set token-level rate limits, model overrides, and quota windows per key.
[01:42] Dana (Product): So if we want to give a partner just generate-key and limit them to X QPS and monthly tokens?
[01:50] Marco: Exactly. You can set a steady-state QPS plus burst capacity, and you can map that to billing if you want to charge partners. We also have org-level defaults that apply if a project doesn't set anything.
[02:05] Priya: How do you handle sudden spikes? For example, our scheduling service could spike at 10x during mornings — we need graceful degradation, not hard shutdowns.
[02:16] Marco: We do soft-fail policies — priority is given based on route and key tier. You can configure fallback model variants or enforced latency SLOs. For bursts there's a burst bucket that you can size per project, and when exhausted the system will either queue or return 429 depending on policy.
[02:34] Marcus: Is queueing maintained at the VPC level for private deployments? We need to keep traffic inside our VPC for pilot.
[02:43] Marco: For Private deployments yes queueing is inside your deployment—there's no egress to Redwood. For Hosted, the queueing is managed by Redwood runtime but it's encrypted in transit and at rest. We'll include network diagrams.
[02:58] Tom (Legal): Quick Q on logs: do you redact prompt text by default? Our legal team will push back on retention of PHI in transcripts.
[03:08] Marco: Good call. By default hosted retention keeps logs for 30 days, prompts are stored unless you enable prompt redaction. For Private we give options to disable storing prompts entirely and ship logs to your SIEM. We'll send the SOC2 and retention options in the security pack.
[03:25] Jenna: I'll follow up — action item to send security docs.
[03:30] Marco: Back to the console — here's an example project config, see rate limit panel: you can set per-minute, per-second, monthly token caps, and a priority class. You can also link a billing code so usage feeds back to your internal chargeback.
[03:48] Marco: Now API side: when you create a project key you get a header like X-Redwood-Org and X-Redwood-Project, or you can use project-scoped API tokens. In code you pass the project key; the runtime enforces the quotas at request time.
[04:05] Priya: Is it possible to do per-customer user limits inside a project, like per clinic ID?
[04:12] Marco: We have sub-keys and metering tags — you can attach a clinic_id tag to requests and apply soft-limits via policy-based quotas. It's not a hard multi-tenant isolation unless you map each clinic to its own project key. So for strict isolation we'd recommend separate project keys per tenant.
[04:32] Marcus: That increases management overhead. Do you provide key rotation and automated key lifecycle?
[04:39] Marco: Yes key rotation via the API, and you can have ephemeral keys too. We have SDK calls to rotate or revoke. The console also shows key age and last-use with clickable revoke.
[04:51] Dana: Walk me through how billing attribution looks.
[04:56] Marco: Usage is attributed at the project key level. The console has a per-project breakdown of tokens, cost, latency. You can export CSVs and wire that into your billing system. There are also tags for SSO groups that we can map.
[05:12] Priya: Any limits on number of projects? We run lots of microservices.
[05:17] Jenna: No hard limit for Dedicated or Private; hosted free tier has some guardrails but it's flexible for enterprise.
[05:25] Priya: Excellent.
[05:30] [05:30] Marco: Quick demo of a rate-limit breach: sending a rapid burst (simulated) — you can see 429s and the console flagging throttled requests with metrics. Note the top right we have a policy that automatically routes to a cheaper model variant when a threshold is crossed, so critical routes can fall back instead of failing.
[05:52] Marcus: That routing is per-route? So we can say for route /summarize use gpt-lite fallback?
[06:00] Marco: Yes you can bind rules to routes or model groups. Keep in mind model variants may have different latency and quality profiles. We'll show Optimize recommendations later.
[06:12] Priya: About the model fallback — we need to ensure output quality thresholds are respected. Can we set QA checks and fallback only if quality stays within a threshold?
[06:22] Marco: We integrate with Redwood Optimize — you can set a quality delta and only fallback if the delta is small; otherwise route to a degraded-but-safe modal or queue. The Optimize engine can also suggest quantization/variant profiles by workload.
[06:38] Jenna: Quick interjection — customers often want examples of SLA language. We have a sample SLA for Dedicated; I'll attach that.
[06:47] Tom: Please do, we need that for procurement.
[06:50] Marco: Now, showing project-level quotas: monthly tokens, daily caps, and per-user QPS. You can also set hard quota vs soft alert. Soft alert will notify and start throttling at a grace level.
[07:08] Marco: (typing) Also, here is the API payload example to set quotas programmatically. It's JSON; I'll paste: {"project_id": "clinic-portal", "quotas": {"monthly_tokens": 2000000, "burst_qps": 200, "steady_qps": 20}} (note: transcription of payload may be imperfect)
[07:33] Priya: For our pilot we expect ~1k QPS steady across all clinics and 5k peak in a 15m window during mornings. Would that be a problem?
[07:44] Marcus: Yes numbers matter for sizing GPUs.
[07:47] Marco: 1k steady / 5k peak is doable on Dedicated; we'd size nodes and set autoscaling + burst buckets. For Hosted we'd recommend Dedicated if you need that predictability. There's also a dedicated burst pool option if you want cost-efficiency with guaranteed burst headroom.
[08:06] Priya: Cost-wise, ballpark?
[08:10] Jenna: I'll put together a committed capacity vs usage-based comparison — that'll be in the pricing sheet I send.
[08:17] Dana: On the private deployment — we want to keep data in-region and use our KMS. How do keys get managed?
[08:25] Marco: For Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; keys for model-serving TLS and at-rest encryption are customer-controlled. We can also set up audit logging to push to your CloudWatch or Splunk.
[08:39] Marcus: Do you support BYOK for model keys?
[08:42] Marco: Yes BYOK is supported in Private mode and for certain Dedicated configs. We'll include the exact posture in the security docs.
[08:52] [08:52] Marco: Now I'll show the runtime behavior under overload. Simulating a degraded node — the smart router will send traffic to other capacity if available, or will apply per-key rate limiting. The console shows per-shard utilization and when eviction happens.
[09:10] Priya: How are rate limits enforced across a multi-region deployment? We have traffic hitting US-east and EU-west.
[09:18] Marco: Rate limits are enforced per-region for latency-sensitive routing, but you can set global quotas as well. We recommend local quotas plus a global soft cap to prevent cross-region burst amplification.
[09:33] Marcus: For PCI/PHI concerns we might use EU-only for European clinics. Can you scope projects to region?
[09:40] Marco: Yes you can pin a project to a region and the control plane enforces routing. For Private you'd deploy in-region.
[09:48] Dana: A quick off-script question: do you have org/project key templates for common roles like analytics vs frontend?
[09:55] Marco: We do. You can apply templates that pre-set quotas and model access. There are built-in templates: dev, staging, production, partner-limited.
[10:05] Priya: Headcount question — how many people at Redwood will we be working with during onboarding?
[10:10] Jenna: Typically AE + SE for onboarding and a customer success manager assigned after contract. For Dedicated/Private we include a launch engineer for the initial deployment.
[10:20] Priya: Perfect.
[10:23] [10:23] Marco: Switching to API error handling: we return 429 with a Retry-After header; we also provide client libraries that implement exponential backoff and jitter patterns. There are SDK helpers to handle token bucketing and local compensating queues.
[10:40] Marcus: Does SDK handle KV cache priming or is that on us?
[10:45] Marco: KV cache priming is managed by the runtime for active contexts, but you can send pre-warm hints; wording sometimes shows up in docs as KV cash — sorry transcribe error — it's KV cache.
[10:57] Dana: Haha noted.
[11:00] Priya: Can we run a quick example of creating a project key via API?
[11:06] Marco: Sure. (pastes) POST /orgs/{org}/projects -> returns project_id and project_key. Then call /quota to set quotas. I'll paste a cURL in the chat after.
[11:18] Jenna: We'll also include a quickstart script for rotating keys and automating per-tenant provisioning. Plenty of customers integrate with SCM for key secrets.
[11:29] Marcus: On rate-limits monitoring — do you have alerting hooks? We want to create PagerDuty alerts when throttling exceeds X% of requests.
[11:38] Marco: Yes alerts and webhooks; you can set thresholds on throttled percent, latency SLO breaches, or queue depth. We can push to PagerDuty, Slack, or your monitoring endpoints.
[11:51] Priya: Ok real-talk: what are common pitfalls customers hit implementing project-key multi-tenant approach?
[11:58] Marco: Three things: too coarse granularity (using one key for too many tenants), not provisioning burst headroom, and not having clear revocation/rotation practices. We give templates and automation to avoid those.
[12:12] Dana: Can we do ephemeral keys for partners that expire after 24h?
[12:17] Marco: Yes, ephemeral tokens are supported and good for limited partner access.
[12:21] Tom: For contract — we need clarity on data residency, log retention, and indemnity. We'll review the security pack.
[12:29] Jenna: Yep will send.
[12:33] Marco: Quick note on quotas — you can export policy as JSON and commit to Git for audit.
[12:40] Priya: That helps from our compliance side.
[12:43] [12:43] Marco: Now a short demo of the Optimize suggestions — here's a workload profile for a hypothetical summarization route. Optimize recommends batching / prefix caching and suggests a quantized model variant that reduces cost by ~30% while keeping quality within an accepted delta. You can accept suggestions and apply them to a project or route.
[13:06] Priya: If we apply those suggestions will it change latency? What's the tradeoff?
[13:11] Marco: Slightly higher token latency, sometimes a few ms depending on kernel paths, but throughput improves and cost drops. We include per-route dashboards so you can A/B the change.
[13:22] Marcus: For the pilot, we want to keep percent error under 1% for critical routes. Is that something Optimize can guard?
[13:30] Marco: You can attach eval sets and set regression alerts so if quality drops beyond a threshold you'll get rollback triggers.
[13:39] Dana: Nice.
[13:41] [13:41] Jenna: We're at about 20 minutes in; let's recap and outline the pilot. Proposed pilot: 2-week staging run on Dedicated minimal nodes with test load that simulates your morning spike, Redwood provides config and help sizing, Lakeshore provides expected QPS and test scripts. After pilot we'll review metrics and tweak quotas.
[14:00] Priya: Sounds right, and we want to run the pilot in our VPC if possible.
[14:05] Marco: Private deployment is best for full VPC-internal. For pilot we can do a Dedicated instance in your cloud region with VPC peering, or a Private eval depending on timeline.
[14:16] Marcus: Timeline? We want procurement to sign by end of October ideally.
[14:22] Jenna: If procurement signs in early October we can start the pilot mid-October. I'll coordinate with Tom on contract terms.
[14:31] Tom: Will do.
[14:34] [14:34] Marco: Quick Q on instrumentation — what observability stack do you use?
[14:39] Marcus: Datadog + Splunk for logs.
[14:43] Marco: We have direct integrations to Datadog and can forward logs to Splunk. For Hosted we can redact prompts; for Private you can forward raw logs.
[14:55] Priya: Great.
[15:00] Dana: Any limitations on number of project keys if we spin up thousands for per-clinic isolation?
[15:06] Marco: No technical limit for Dedicated/Private; management overhead is the main cost. We recommend using automation templates and lifecycle rules to rotate and repeal old keys.
[15:18] Jenna: Ok, we're about 25 minutes in, Marco do you want to show the example config we'll send?
[15:24] Marco: Sure — I'll paste the sample policy and the console screenshots in the follow-up.
[15:30] [15:30] Marco: (brief silence) One design note: when using project keys for billing, you can also configure a soft quota that alerts before hitting a hard cap — customers often set 80% alert tier.
[15:45] Priya: We'll want that.
[15:48] Marcus: Anything else on compliance?
[15:51] Marco: Nothing new, we'll send the SOC2/ISO pack and KMS docs.
[15:56] Jenna: Final quick ask — Marcus could you send expected QPS and top 20 routes so Marco can prep sizing?
[16:04] Marcus: Yep will do by next Monday.
[16:07] Jenna: Great. Recap of next steps: Jenna send pricing and SLA samples; Marco send security pack and sample configs; Marcus send traffic profile; Tom coordinate contract clauses. I'll propose follow-up slots for procurement.
[16:20] Priya: Thanks, this was helpful, appreciate the thoroughness.
[16:24] Marco: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with artifacts.
[16:28] Tom: Thanks.

End of transcript

References in chat: I'll paste links in the follow-up: console screenshots, sample quota JSON, SOC2 pack (link), Quickstart script GitHub gist (link).
